Abstract: The addition of radicals to unsaturated precur-
sors is ap owerful tool for the synthesis of both carbo-
and heterocyclic organic building blocks. The recent
advento fm ild ways to generate N-centered radicals has
reignited interest in exploiting highly regio-, chemo-,a nd
stereoselective transformationst hat employ these reactive
intermediates. While the additions of aminyl, iminyl, and
amidylr adicals to alkenes and alkynes have been well-
studied, analogous additions to allenesa re scarce. Allenes
offer several attractive features, including potentialf or se-
lective amidation at three distinct sites via judicious
choice of precursor or radical source, the opportunityf or
axial-to-pointc hirality transfer,a nd productivet rappingo f
vinyl or allyl radical intermediates to diversify functionality
in the products.I nt his article,w er eport ar egioselective
additiono fa midyl radicals to allenes to furnisha na rray of
valuable N-heterocycle scaffolds.
Since the first report of the triphenylmethyl radical by Moses
Gombergi n1 900, reactions involving radical intermediates
have become important tools for the efficient functionalization
of organic molecules.[1] Ar ecent renaissance in radical chemis-
try has resulted in several mild strategies to generate and ex-
ploit these reactive intermediates, including N-centered radi-
cals.[2] While the additionso fN -radicals to alkenes and alkynes
have been well-studied,t he analogousr egio- and stereo-con-
trolled additions of these species to allenes are underdevel-
oped.[3] This is despite the potential for the expedientc on-
struction of N-heterocycles that appear in pharmaceuticals,
agrochemicals, natural products, and materials.
Allenesc ontain two cumulated, orthogonal p-bonds and
three distinct sites for potentiallyt unable addition of aN -radi-
cal species. Allenes also typicallyd isplay higher reactivity than
their alkene counterparts, as well as greater thermodynamic
stabilityc ompared to the corresponding alkynes.M ost interest-
ingly,r adical addition to aa llene can occur at the proximal a
carbon( Scheme 1B )t og enerate av inyl radical, at the b
carbont of urnish an allyl radical, or at the other g carbon to
yield an endocyclic vinyl radical. While formation of the stabi-
lized allyl radical might be expected to be preferred, the ortho-
gonality of the two p-systems meanst hat stabilization of this
radical requires a9 08 rotation;t his additional energy require-
ment can often result in the favorable kinetic formation of a
vinyl radical instead.[3a, 4] This vinyl radicalc an be trapped with
av ariety of electrophiles to introduce additional functionality
into the products or participate downstream in radical cascade
reactions.
Nitrogen-centered radicals come in av arietyo f“ flavors”,
with the overall reactivitiesb roadly categorized as nucleophilic,
electrophilic, or ambiphilic.[2b] Amidyl radicals are popular for

where the use of either am etal or organic photocatalyst fur-

Our laboratory’s interesti nn ew methods for stereo-con-
trolled C@Nb ond formation,c oupled with the potential of al-
lenes as radical acceptors, prompted us to investigate whether
regioselective amidyl radicala ddition to allenesc ould be ach-
ieved with concomitant modification to all three unsaturated
carbonso ft he allene.P reliminary studies exploredt he influ-
ence of the precursor substitution pattern, the tether length
between the nitrogen and the allene, the electronic features of
the radical, and the reaction conditions on the regioselectivity
of addition of the N-centered radicalt ot he allene.E stablishing
these general trends will ultimately enable these reactivities to
be harnessed to furnisha na rray of powerful scaffolds for the
syntheses of valuable N-heterocycles (Scheme 1B )t hat are
complementary to transition metal and ionic-based protocols.
Herein, we report am ild, catalyst-free addition of amidyl radi-
cals to allenes that proceeds with high regioselectivityf or addi-
tion to the a site to generate intermediate vinyl radicals that
can be trapped with diversee lectrophiles.
We began our investigationse mploying electrophilica midyl
radicals, whicht ot he best of our knowledgeh ave not been
studied in terms of their reactivity towards allenes. These radi-
cals are typically generatedv ia functionalization of an amide
nitrogen with ar adicalp recursor group (RPG), followed by ho-
molyticc leavage of the N-RPG bond in the presence of ar adi-
cal initiator,h eat, irradiation, and/or ap hotocatalyst (PC).[5–7]
Photochemical generation of amidyl radicals is particularly at-
tractive, as this strategy avoids the use of toxic initiators and
harsh reaction conditions.
The Leonori group has popularized aryloxyamides as precur-
sors to amidyl radicals using Eosin Ya st he photocatalyst
(Scheme 1A ). This strategy is attractive, as it avoids the use of
rare noble metals and strong oxidants that might engage in
undesired reactionw ith the allene moiety.[8] Inspired by this
work, aryloxyamide 1a was prepared and subjected it to visi-
ble light irradiation( Table 1). Irradiation of 1a using a1 3W
green LED in the presenceo fE osin Y, K2CO3,a nd 1,4-cyclohexa-
diene (1,4-CHD) as the H-atom donor in acetone furnished
41 %o ft he 5-exo-trig cyclization product 2a as am ixture of
stereoisomers (entry 1). To our surprise, 18 %o f 2a was ob-
served even in the absence of Eosin Y( entry 2). While the UV-
vis spectrum of 1a indicates a lmax < 350 nm, the fact that irra-
diation with green LED and CFL (see the Supporting Informa-
tion for details) furnishes 2a prompted us to try other light
sourcest oi mprovey ields without the need for Eosin Y. Irradia-
tion at 440 nm (see the Supporting Information for wave-
lengths screened) significantly improved the yield of 2a to
78 %( entry 4). While dilution from 0.1 m in acetone (entry 3) to
0.025 m (entry 4) did not change the yield or E:Z ratio, it did
shorten the reactiont ime. Presumably,d ecrease reaction time
is the result of increaset ransparency of the reactionm ixture.
DMSO and MeCN (entry 5) were also effective solvents (see the
Supporting Information for ac omplete solvent screen). The
1,4-CHDc ould be replacedw ith other hydrogen atom donors,
including 9,10-dihydroanthracene (9,10-DHA) and Hantzsch
ester (entries 6–7). Attempts to increaset he E:Z ratio by em-
ploying bulky H-donors delivered lower yields with no increase
in stereoselectivity (see Supporting Information for complete
list of H-donors screened).
Controle xperiments (entries 8–9) demonstratec yclization

1,4-CHD( entry 10) gave 49 %o f 2a ,w ith 37 %s howing D-in-
corporation from the solvent. As expected, removing both 1,4-
CHD andK 2CO3 from the mixture (entry 11)r esulted in no reac-
tion to 2a .D ecreasing the temperature to @20 8C( entry 12)
and @40 8C( entry 13) led to less competing reduction of the
amidyl radical to 3a [9] and improved both yield and E:Z ratio.
Notably,n oH -atom abstraction product 3a was observeda t

was investigated (Table 2). Several substrates with at hree-
carbon tetherb etween the nitrogen and allene were investi-
gated. In these cases, 5-exo-trig cyclization is expectedt ob e

electronic prerequisites for radicala ddition to a p-bond.[10]

The influence of the tether length between the allene and

Carbamatesw ere tolerated under the reactions conditions
and led to 1,2- and 1,3-cyclic carbamates 2j –2l .I na greement

The intermediate vinyl radical could be trapped with other
electrophiles in addition to hydrogen atom donors. Employing
an excess of the radicalt rapping agents N-chlorosuccinimide
(NCS), trimethoxyphospine, diethylb romomalonate, and N-
(phenylseleno)phthalimide furnished the functionalized alkenes

molecular trapping agents, including Michael acceptors, O2

While ap hotocatalyst is not required, we were curiousa st o
why K2CO3 is key to successful reaction. Initial insights into the
role of this additivew ere carried out by varying both the
anion and cation of the salt (selected results in Table 4). KCl
(entry 1) gave lower reactivity and yield, while KHCO3 (entry 2)
and other potassium salts (see Supporting Information for de-
tails) performed similarly to K2CO3,a lbeit with prolongedr eac-
tion times.T he lack of ac lear trend between the salt’s basicity
and yield and/orr eaction time argues against it serving solely
as aB rønsted base. Cs (entry 5) and Li (entry 6) carbonates
gave similar results to K2CO3,a lthough Na2CO3 gave al ower
yield (entry 7). The higher solubility of Cs2CO3 and tetrabuty-
lammonium acetate (entries 5, 8) reduced the reaction time
compared to K2CO3.F inally,d ecreasing the K2CO3 to 0.2 equiva-
lents (entry 9) still gave 83 %y ield of 2a after 5.6 h. Taken to-
gether,t hese results cannot rule out the role of the salt as a
simple electrolyte, where irradiation at 440 nm directly excited
1a to promote either direct homolysis of the N@Ob ond or a
SET event that initiates formation of the amidyl radical.
The intermediacy of radical species was supported by
adding TEMPOt ot he reactiont og ive the trapped product 2a -
T,a sd etected by both mass spectrometry and 1HN MR analysis
of the crude reaction( Scheme 2). The fact that 14 %o f 1a re-
mains after 1.5 ho fi rradiationa rgues against direct breaking
of the weak N@Ob ond, as complete cleavagew ould be ex-
pected in the presenceo fT EMPO under the reaction condi-
tions.
Another possibility involves formation of an exciplex com-
plex between the allene and the RPG,a ss imilar mechanisms
have been proposed in other radical additions to allenes.[15] To
rule out the likehood of an allene exciplex complex, the amidyl
radicalp recusor 6 was employed (Scheme 3). Under the reac-
tion conditions, the H-atom abstraction product 7 was ob-
served, providing evidence against an exciplexc omplex involv-
ing the allene as necessary fort he N@Ob ond cleavage.
Finally,U V-vis experiments were carriedo ut to assess the po-
tential for formation of an electron donor-acceptor (EDA) com-
plex. Ar ecent report by Peric/sd escribed aE DA complex be-
tween K2CO3 and an electron-poor aryl group, based on the
changes in absorption of different components.[8e] In our
system,a slight difference in the UV/Vis spectra of 1a in ace-
tone and 1a /K2CO3 in acetone( red andb lack traces, respec-
tively,F igure1 )w as observed. In contrast, whenK 2SO4 was
used as the donor,n oc hange in absorbance between 1a in
acetonea nd 1a /K2SO4 in acetonew as noted (see the SI for
more details). Indeed, employing K2SO4 as the donor insteado f
K2CO3 under optimized conditions (Table 4, entry 3) gave no
cyclized product 2a .
Am echanism was proposed based on our preliminaryf ind-
ings (Scheme 4). An EDA complex forms from 1a and the
donor K2CO3 (D). Irradiationo f A results in aS ET event to yield
B,w hich fragments to furnish C and D.T hree possible fates of
C/D include:( 1) Direct reduction of D to 3a ;( 2) 5-exo-trig cycli-
zation to give E-a nd Z-isomers of intermediate E,o r( 3) dimeri-
zation of the amidyl radical (not detected). Trapping of inter-
mediates E-(Z) and E-(E) furnishes 2a .A catalytic amount of
K2CO3 can be utilized, as it is proposed to be turned over by a
SET event with the radical from H-atom abstraction from 1,4-
CHD or with an aryloxy fragment. Finally,a lights on/off experi-
ment indicatedn egligible conversion when the light was off
and no isomerization of 2a -(E/Z) once formed (see the Sup-
porting Information ford etails).

In conclusion, we have developeda direct and regioselective
addition of amidyl radicals to allenest of urnish highly modifia-
ble g-lactams that can serve as scaffolds for drugs and natural
products.V arious substitution patterns are well-tolerated and
diversee lectrophiles can be used to trap the intermediate
vinyl radicals. Ongoing investigations are targeted towards
methods that deliver products where all three allene carbons
are functionalized, as well as experimental and computational
studies of other radicala dditions to allenest oa chieve com-
plexity-forming cascade reactions.
